title: Roman school: justification includes real abolition and infused righteousness
source_text: XXVII. Doctores vero Ecclesiae Romanae justificandi vocem in Scholis suis aliter usurpant. Nec enim apud eos justificatio designat solam poenae peccato debitae condonationem, sed praeterea realem peccati abolitionem, & internae cujusdam justitiae adeptionem. Et sic, ex eorum sensu, dicitur justificari, non solum qui a peccati reatu absolvitur, sed cui justitia de novo infunditur, aut qui in accepta jam ante justitia progreditur & crescit. Unde duplex apud eos distinguitur justificatio, prima scilicet, & secunda. Prima, per quam aliquis ex peccatore, injusto, & impio, sanctus & justus efficitur. Secunda vero per quam, qui ante justus erat, ex justo fit justior, & quoddam justitiae incrementum accipit. Sed quum de justificatione simpliciter loquuntur, ordinarie primam intelligunt, quae ex eorum usu justificatio impii dici solet.
pass_a_gloss: But the Doctors of the Roman Church use the word of justifying otherwise in their Schools. For among them justification does not designate only the condonation of the penalty due to sin, but besides that a real abolition of sin and the obtaining of a certain inward righteousness. And so, in their sense, one is said to be justified not only who is absolved from the guilt of sin, but to whom righteousness is infused anew, or who progresses and grows in righteousness already received before. Whence a double justification is distinguished among them, namely first and second. The first, by which someone from a sinner, unjust, and impious is made holy and just. But the second, by which he who was just before becomes more just from just, and receives a certain increase of righteousness. But when they speak of justification simply, they ordinarily understand the first, which in their usage is wont to be called the justification of the ungodly.
pass_b_english: Romans: justification = not only penalty remitted but sin abolished and inward righteousness obtained.
First vs second justification: make the ungodly just; then make the just more just.

choices.why: Roman formal cause of first justification.
